l: Haman's plot to destroy the people (plot against Esther's people), Esther (Greek), Chapter 7
s: Esther exposes the plot to the king, describing it as the sale of her people for destruction, pillage, and genocide, and names Haman as the enemy behind it. The plot ends with Haman's hanging.

l: Esther (Greek), Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: King Ahasuerus gives Esther all that belonged to Haman, and Mordecai receives the king's ring and is appointed over Haman's former holdings. Esther pleads again, falling at the king's feet, and asks that Haman's letters against the Jews be reversed. The king tells her to write in his name whatever seems good and seal it with his ring. On the twenty-third day of Nisan the scribes write orders to the governors of 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia, permitting the Jews to use their own laws and defend themselves against attackers on the thirteenth day of Adar. The text of the letter denounces Haman, and Mordecai goes out in royal apparel while the Jews rejoice and many Gentiles are circumcised and become Jews for fear of them.

l: King Ahasuerus, Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: King Ahasuerus gives Esther Haman's possessions, gives Mordecai the ring taken from Haman, and extends the golden sceptre to Esther. He tells Esther and Mordecai to write in his name and seal with his ring, since such writings cannot be countermanded, and his name is on the letter sent to the provinces permitting the Jews to defend themselves.

l: Esther, Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: Esther receives all that belonged to Haman, appoints Mordecai over it, and again pleads with the king, falling at his feet, to reverse Haman's letters. She says she cannot bear to see the affliction of her people and kindred. The king authorizes her to write in his name.

l: Haman, Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: Haman's possessions are given to Esther and his ring is taken from him and given to Mordecai. The king's letter calls him a Macedonian, son of Hammedatha, an alien to the Persians, who plotted against the king, Mordecai, Esther, and the Jews and to transfer the Persian dominion to the Macedonians. The letter states he was hanged with his whole family at the gates of Susa.

l: Mordecai, Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: Mordecai is called before the king, who gives him the ring taken from Haman, and Esther appoints him over all that had been Haman's. He goes out in royal apparel with a golden crown and a diadem of fine purple linen, and the people of Susa rejoice. The king's letter calls him a deliverer and perpetual benefactor.

l: Jews, Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: The Jews are granted the right to use their own laws, help each other, and defend themselves on the thirteenth day of Adar against those who attack them. They are told to be ready for that day, and the letter calls them sons of the living God who live by just laws. In every city and province they have light, gladness, feasting and mirth, and many Gentiles are circumcised and become Jews for fear of them.

l: letters sent by Haman, Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: Esther asks that the letters Haman sent, written for the destruction of the Jews in the kingdom, be reversed. The king's letter instructs the provinces to refuse to obey them.

l: king's letter of reversal, Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: The scribes write the letter on the twenty-third day of Nisan, seal it with the king's ring, and send it by couriers and horsemen to 127 provinces in their own languages. It denounces Haman, orders the Jews allowed to use their own customs and defend themselves on the thirteenth of Adar, and calls for a day of festivity. It threatens any city or province that does not comply with destruction by spear and fire, and copies are posted publicly and published in Susa.

l: enemies of the Jews, Esther (Greek), Chapter 8
s: The Jews are permitted to treat their adversaries and those who attack them as they please on the thirteenth day of Adar. The king's letter says that for those who plotted against the king this day is a memorial of destruction, and the Jews are told to be ready to fight their enemies.

l: Esther (Greek), Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: On the thirteenth of Adar the king's letters arrived and the Jews' adversaries perished, since no one resisted out of fear of the Jews and of Mordecai. In Susa the Jews killed five hundred men, including the ten sons of Haman, and the king, hearing this, asked Esther what more she wanted. Esther requested a second day of the same action in Susa and the hanging of Haman's sons' bodies, which the king allowed; the Jews of Susa killed three hundred more on the fourteenth, while the Jews elsewhere destroyed fifteen thousand, taking no spoil. Mordecai then wrote to all the Jews of Ahasuerus's kingdom establishing the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar as days of feasting, joy, and gifts to friends and the poor, named Purim after the lots Haman cast. Mordecai and Esther confirmed this observance by letter and command as a memorial to be kept forever.

l: Jews, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: The Jews killed five hundred men in Susa on the first day and three hundred more on the fourteenth, while those elsewhere in the kingdom destroyed fifteen thousand, taking no spoil. They then rested and celebrated with joy and gladness. They consented to Mordecai's letter and took on the keeping of Purim for themselves and their descendants in every generation.

l: Mordecai, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Mordecai was feared by the officials, which led them to honor the Jews. He wrote the account in a book and sent it to all the Jews near and far, establishing the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar as days of feasting and gifts. Together with Esther he confirmed the Purim decision, pledging their own well-being to it.

l: Esther, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Esther, asked by the king what more she wanted, requested that the Jews be allowed to do the same the next day and that Haman's sons' bodies be hanged. She is called the daughter of Aminadab. With Mordecai she wrote and confirmed the letter about Purim and established it by a command forever.

l: Haman, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Haman is identified as the son of Hammedatha, called the Bugaean and, in Mordecai's letter, the Macedonian, and as the enemy of the Jews. The letter recounts how he decreed and cast lots to destroy them and sought Mordecai's hanging. His calamities fell on himself, and he was hanged along with his children.

l: King Ahasuerus, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Ahasuerus, the king, saw his letters arrive and his order take force on the thirteenth of Adar. He heard the Susa death toll and asked Esther what more she wished. He permitted the second day of killing and gave the bodies of Haman's sons to the Jews to hang. His kingdom is the one to which Mordecai sent the Purim letter.

l: sons of Haman, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: The ten sons of Haman are named as Pharsannes, Delphon, Phasga, Pharadatha, Barea, Sarbaca, Marmasima, Ruphaeus, Arsaeus, and Zabuthaeus. They were among those killed in Susa, and their property was plundered. At Esther's request their bodies were given to the Jews to be hanged.

l: Susa, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: In Susa the Jews killed five hundred men on the first day, including Haman's ten sons, and the toll was reported to the king. The Jews there assembled again on the fourteenth and killed three hundred more, taking no property. They rested and celebrated on the fourteenth and fifteenth.

l: Adar, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Adar is the twelfth month, in which the king's letters arrived on the thirteenth day. The thirteenth was the day of the killing, and the fourteenth, and in Susa the fifteenth, became days of rest and joy. The whole month is described as one in which mourning turned to joy and sorrow to a holiday.

l: Purim, Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Purim is the name given to the days of the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar because of the lots Haman cast, and because of the words of Mordecai's letter and all the Jews suffered. It was established as a memorial to be kept forever in every generation, city, family, and province, with feasting, gladness, gifts to friends and portions to the poor. Mordecai and Esther confirmed it by letter and command.

l: killing of enemies (by the Jews), Esther (Greek), Chapter 9
s: On the thirteenth of Adar the adversaries of the Jews perished, with no one resisting out of fear. Five hundred were killed in Susa, then three hundred more there the next day at Esther's request, and fifteen thousand elsewhere in the kingdom. The Jews took no spoil except in the first Susa killing, where the sons of Haman's property was plundered.

l: Esther (Greek), Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: Chapter 10 opens with King Ahasuerus levying a tax on land and sea, and notes that his strength and glory are recorded in the book of the Persians and Medes. Mordecai is described as viceroy to the king, a great man honored by the Jews and loved by his nation. In a bracketed passage, Mordecai says these events came from God and interprets his earlier dream: the spring that became a river is Esther, the two serpents are Haman and himself, and the nations are those who sought to destroy the Jews. He says God ordained two lots, one for his people and one for the other nations, delivered Israel, and commanded that the days of the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar be observed forever. The chapter closes with a note that Dositheus and his son Ptolemeus brought the letter of Purim to Egypt in the fourth year of Ptolemeus and Cleopatra, and that Lysimachus in Jerusalem had interpreted it.

l: King Ahasuerus, Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: King Ahasuerus levies a tax on his kingdom by land and sea. His strength, valour, wealth and glory are said to be written in the book of the Persians and Medes. Mordecai serves as his viceroy, and Esther is the woman he married and made queen.

l: Mordecai, Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: Mordecai is called viceroy to King Ahasuerus, a great man honored by the Jews and loved by his whole nation. He declares that these events came from God and interprets his dream, identifying himself and Haman as the two serpents.

l: Esther, Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: In Mordecai's interpretation, Esther is the little spring that became a river, the woman whom the king married and made queen.

l: Haman, Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: Haman is identified in Mordecai's interpretation of the dream as one of the two serpents, the other being Mordecai.

l: God, Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: Mordecai attributes all these events to God, who delivered Israel, rescued them from calamities, and worked signs and great wonders not seen among the nations. God ordained two lots, one for his people and one for the other nations, and remembered his people and vindicated his inheritance.

l: Jews, Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: The Jews honor Mordecai, and he is loved by all his nation. They are identified with Israel, who cried to God and were delivered, while the nations combined to destroy the name of the Jews. They are to observe the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar with assembly, joy and gladness throughout the generations.

l: Mordecai's vision, Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: Mordecai recalls his dream and says not one detail has failed. He explains its elements: the spring that became a river is Esther, the two serpents are Haman and himself, the nations are those who combined to destroy the Jews, and his nation is Israel. The two lots correspond to the one for God's people and the one for the other nations.

l: Purim, Esther (Greek), Chapter 10
s: The days of observance are set for the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, with assembly, joy and gladness before God, forever among Israel. In the fourth year of Ptolemeus and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said he was a priest and Levite, and his son Ptolemeus brought this letter of Purim, which they said was authentic and which Lysimachus son of Ptolemeus in Jerusalem had interpreted.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 recounts how Alexander the Macedonian, son of Philip, defeated Darius, conquered much of the earth, and on his deathbed divided his kingdom among his servants, who ruled after him and multiplied evils. From them came Antiochus Epiphanes, who reigned in the 137th year of the Greeks. Under him, transgressors of the law in Israel made a covenant with the Gentiles, built a gymnasium in Jerusalem, and abandoned circumcision. Antiochus conquered Egypt, then plundered the Jerusalem temple, and two years later his chief tribute collector deceitfully attacked and burned the city and fortified the city of David as a citadel. Antiochus decreed that all be one people and forsake their own laws, banned sacrifices, the Sabbath, and circumcision on pain of death, set up an abomination of desolation on the altar, and burned the books of the law, yet many in Israel chose death rather than eat unclean food, and great wrath came upon Israel.

l: Alexander, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Alexander, son of Philip from the land of Chittim, struck Darius king of the Persians and Medes and reigned in his place over Greece. He fought many battles, took strongholds, killed kings, and collected tribute from many nations until he fell sick. He divided his kingdom among his servants while still alive, reigned twelve years, and died.

l: Alexander's servants, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Alexander's honorable servants, raised with him from youth, received his kingdom from him before his death and each ruled in his place. They all put crowns on themselves after he died, as did their sons for many years, and they multiplied evils on the earth. From them came the sinful root Antiochus Epiphanes.

l: King Antiochus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Antiochus Epiphanes, son of King Antiochus and a former hostage at Rome, reigned from the 137th year of the Greeks. He invaded Egypt, defeated Ptolemy, then returned to plunder Jerusalem and its temple. Later he decreed that all his kingdom become one people, forsake their own laws, and obey on pain of death, and he enforced pagan worship in Judah.

l: Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Israel was divided, as some of its people embraced Gentile ways while many others suffered. It endured great mourning after the temple was plundered, then slaughter, captivity, and a decree forbidding its worship and law. Many consented to Antiochus's worship, but many resolved not to eat unclean things and chose to die, and exceedingly great wrath came upon Israel.

l: transgressors of the law (Israel), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Transgressors of the law came out of Israel and persuaded many to make a covenant with the Gentiles, believing separation had brought evils. Some went to the king, who authorized them to follow Gentile ordinances, so they built a gymnasium in Jerusalem, made themselves uncircumcised, forsook the holy covenant, and sold themselves to do evil. Later a sinful nation of transgressors of the law was placed in the city of David citadel.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem received a Gentile-style gymnasium, was entered and plundered by Antiochus, and two years later was attacked suddenly after words of peace from his chief collector of tribute. The city was spoiled, burned, and its houses and walls pulled down, its women and children taken captive, and the city of David fortified as a hostile citadel. Its inhabitants fled and it became a habitation of foreigners, with its feasts turned to mourning and its Sabbaths to reproach.

l: sanctuary, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Antiochus entered the sanctuary presumptuously and took the golden altar, lampstand, table of show bread, cups, bowls, censers, veil, crowns, and gold decoration. The citadel became a place to lie in wait against it, innocent blood was shed around it, and it was defiled and laid waste like a wilderness. The king's letters ordered its offerings forbidden and the sanctuary polluted.

l: Antiochus's decree, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Antiochus wrote to his whole kingdom that all should be one people and each forsake his own laws, and all the nations agreed. His letters to Jerusalem and Judah forbade burnt offerings, sacrifices, Sabbaths, feasts, and circumcision, and ordered altars, temples, and shrines for idols and the sacrifice of swine and unclean animals. Anyone who did not obey was to die, and he appointed overseers and ordered the cities of Judah to sacrifice.

l: abomination (Antiochus's, on the altar), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: On the fifteenth day of Chislev in the 145th year, an abomination of desolation was built upon the altar. On the twenty-fifth day of the month sacrifice was made upon the idol altar placed on top of the altar of burnt offering. Idol altars were also built in the cities of Judah on every side.

l: plundering of the temple, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: After defeating Egypt in the 143rd year, Antiochus went up against Israel and Jerusalem with a great multitude and entered the sanctuary. He took the golden altar, lampstand, table, cups, bowls, censers, veil, crowns, silver, gold, precious vessels, and hidden treasures, and peeled the gold decoration off the front of the temple. He then went to his own land after making a great slaughter and speaking arrogantly, and great mourning came upon Israel.

l: persecution of Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 1
s: Persecution included slaughter, captivity, burning of Jerusalem, forced sacrifices to idols, and the tearing up and burning of the books of the law. Anyone found with a book of the covenant or consenting to the law was sentenced to death, and women who had circumcised their children were put to death with their babies hung around their necks. Many refused to eat unclean food and died rather than profane the holy covenant.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Mattathias, a priest living at Modin with his five sons, laments the desecration of Jerusalem and the Temple. When the king's officers come to Modin to enforce sacrifice and offer him honors for compliance, he refuses publicly, kills a Jew who steps up to sacrifice along with the king's officer, and tears down the altar, then flees with his sons to the mountains. Many faithful refugees who go into the wilderness are attacked on the Sabbath and about a thousand die without resisting, so Mattathias and his friends decide to fight on the Sabbath if attacked. Joined by the Hasidaeans, they raise an army, strike down sinners, pull down altars, circumcise boys by force, and rescue the law from the Gentiles. Before dying in the 146th year, Mattathias exhorts his sons with examples from Israel's heroes, names Simon as counselor and father and Judas Maccabaeus as captain, and is buried at Modin.

l: Mattathias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Mattathias, a priest of the sons of Joarib living at Modin, mourns the ruin of Jerusalem, refuses the king's officers' offer of honors, and kills an apostate Jew and the king's officer at the altar in zeal like Phinehas. He flees to the mountains, leads the resistance, decides with his friends to fight on the Sabbath, and gives a farewell charge to his sons citing Abraham, Joseph, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, David, Elijah, Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael and Daniel. He blesses them and dies in the 146th year, buried at Modin amid Israel's great lamentation.

l: sons of Mattathias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Mattathias has five sons: John (Gaddis), Simon (Thassi), Judas (Maccabaeus), Eleazar (Avaran) and Jonathan (Apphus). They mourn with their father, flee with him to the mountains, and receive his dying charge to be zealous for the law and give their lives for the covenant; Simon is named their counselor and father, and they bury Mattathias at Modin.

l: Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Judas Maccabaeus is listed as one of Mattathias's five sons. Mattathias declares him strong and mighty from his youth and appoints him captain, to fight the battle of the people.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Jerusalem is lamented by Mattathias as a holy city destroyed, its temple dishonored, vessels carried off, and people slain and enslaved. Its people, including some who remained there, are cited by the king's officers as having complied with the king's command, and the king's forces are stationed in the city of David.

l: Modin, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Modin is the city where Mattathias lives and where the king's officers come to enforce sacrifice. Mattathias kills a Jew and the king's officer there and pulls down the altar, and later he is buried in his ancestors' tombs at Modin.

l: Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Many of Israel gather to the king's officers at Modin, and Israel's mighty men, the Hasidaeans, join Mattathias. Mattathias's company pulls down altars and circumcises uncircumcised boys throughout the coasts of Israel, and all Israel makes great lamentation at his death.

l: king's officers, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: The king's officers enforce the apostasy and come to Modin to compel sacrifice, offering Mattathias honors of silver, gold and the status of the king's friends. After he refuses, one officer is killed by Mattathias, and others pursue the refugees into the wilderness and attack them on the Sabbath.

l: king (the ruler over the Jews), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: The king issues a commandment requiring sacrifice and abandonment of ancestral worship, which all the nations and many in Judah have followed. Mattathias refuses to heed his words, and his officers promise rewards for compliance and pursue those who break his command.

l: Gentiles, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: The Gentiles are described as having profaned Jerusalem's holy things and taken her spoils. Mattathias's company fights to rescue the law from their hand, and apostate Jews flee to them for safety; Mattathias tells his sons to repay them.

l: covenant of the fathers, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Mattathias vows that he, his sons and kindred will walk in the covenant of their fathers and not forsake the law and ordinances. He calls those zealous for the law to follow him, and his army rescues the law from the Gentiles and kings; he charges his sons to give their lives for the covenant.

l: Sabbath, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: The refugees in the wilderness refuse to resist or profane the Sabbath when attacked, and about a thousand die. Mattathias and his friends then resolve to fight anyone who attacks them on the Sabbath.

l: Jewish refugees in the wilderness, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Many who sought justice go into the wilderness with their children, wives and livestock because evils multiplied. The king's forces overtake them and attack on the Sabbath; they refuse to fight or block their hiding places, and about a thousand die, declaring their innocence before heaven and earth.

l: Mattathias's uprising, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: The uprising begins when Mattathias kills the apostate and the king's officer at Modin and flees with his sons. After the Sabbath massacre, they resolve to fight on the Sabbath, are joined by the Hasidaeans and fugitives, and raise an army that strikes sinners and lawless men and pulls down altars. Their work prospers, and the sinner is never allowed to triumph.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Judas Maccabaeus succeeds his father and, with his kindred, fights for Israel, defeating Apollonius and then Seron at the ascent of Bethhoron, where he tells his frightened men that victory comes from heaven rather than numbers. King Antiochus, angered and short of money, leaves for Persia, entrusting half his forces, the elephants, and the charge to destroy Judea to Lysias. Lysias sends Ptolemy, Nicanor, and Gorgias with forty thousand infantry and seven thousand cavalry, who camp near Emmaus while merchants come to buy Israelite captives as slaves. Judas and his people gather at Mizpeh to fast, pray, and consult the book of the law, then organize their ranks, send home those exempted by the law, and camp south of Emmaus. Judas urges his men to be ready to fight, saying it is better to die in battle than to see the nation's and the holy place's calamities, and leaves the outcome to the will of heaven.

l: Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Judas, called Maccabaeus, rises in his father's place and is likened to a lion, hunting the lawless and turning wrath from Israel. He kills Apollonius and keeps his sword, routs Seron at Bethhoron, and assures his fearful men that heaven can save by many or by few. At Mizpeh and Emmaus he appoints captains, sends home those exempted by the law, and exhorts his men to fight, leaving the result to heaven's will.

l: Seron, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Seron, commander of the Syrian army, resolves to make a name for himself by fighting Judas and those who despise the king's command. He marches with a mighty army of the ungodly to the ascent of Bethhoron, where Judas attacks and defeats him.

l: King Antiochus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Antiochus is filled with indignation at Judas's fame and gathers all his forces, paying them a year in advance. Finding his treasury depleted and tribute small because of the unrest he caused, he goes to Persia to collect money, leaving Lysias in charge and taking half the forces. He leaves Antioch in the one hundred forty seventh year and crosses the Euphrates.

l: Lysias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Lysias, described as an honorable man of royal lineage, is left in charge of the king's affairs from the Euphrates to the borders of Egypt and to raise the king's son Antiochus. He receives half the forces and the elephants, and is charged to root out Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem and settle foreigners on their land. He chooses Ptolemy, Nicanor, and Gorgias and sends them with a large army against Judah.

l: Judas's kindred and followers, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Judas's kindred and his father's supporters help him and fight gladly for Israel. At Bethhoron his small, hungry company fears Seron's army but is encouraged by Judas and wins. At Mizpeh they fast and pray, and then are organized into captains of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, with some sent home according to the law.

l: Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Israel is protected and its wrath turned away through Judas's deeds, and nations around begin to fear him. It is now targeted by the king's order to destroy its strength and give its land to foreigners by lot. Its people respond by resolving to repair the ruins of their people and fight for the holy place.

l: Syrian army, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Syrian forces under Seron are defeated at Bethhoron, with about eight hundred killed and the rest fleeing to the land of the Philistines. A far larger force of forty thousand infantry and seven thousand cavalry, led by Ptolemy, Nicanor, and Gorgias, then camps near Emmaus. Forces of Syria and of the Philistines join merchants who come to buy captives.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Jerusalem is described as empty like a wilderness, with none of her offspring going in or out. Foreigners hold the citadel, Gentiles live there, and joy, the pipe, and the harp have ceased. The king's order targets the remnant of Jerusalem for destruction, and the Israelites gather at Mizpeh nearby.

l: Emmaus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Emmaus, in the plain country, is where the Syrian army under Ptolemy, Nicanor, and Gorgias encamps. Merchants and allied forces gather there, and Judas's army later camps on its south side.

l: sanctuary, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: The sanctuary is trampled down and profaned, and children of foreigners hold the citadel. The people cry to heaven about its state and resolve to fight for the holy place. Judas says it is better to die in battle than to see the calamities of the nation and the holy place.

l: God, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Judas says that with heaven it makes no difference whether it saves by many or by few, and that strength comes from heaven, not from a multitude. He says that God himself will crush the enemy. The people cry out to heaven for help at Mizpeh, and Judas leaves the outcome to the will in heaven.

l: Battle of Bethhoron, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Seron's large army meets Judas's small company at the ascent of Bethhoron. After Judas's speech, he rushes suddenly against them and they are defeated. They are pursued down the descent to the plain, about eight hundred fall, and the rest flee to Philistine land, spreading fear of Judas among the nations.

l: fasting and prayer at Mizpeh, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: The Israelites gather at Mizpeh, a former place of prayer for Israel, and fast, wear sackcloth, put ashes on their heads, and tear their clothes. They open the book of the law, bring priestly garments, first fruits, and tithes, and stir up the Nazarites. They cry to heaven for help against the assembled Gentiles, then sound trumpets and shout.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Gorgias leads a night march with five thousand infantry and a thousand cavalry to surprise Judas, but Judas slips past him and defeats the king's army at Emmaus, burning its camp and sending Gorgias' men fleeing to Philistine territory. Lysias, hearing of the defeat, gathers sixty thousand infantry and five thousand cavalry the next year, but Judas meets him at Bethsura with ten thousand men after praying, and about five thousand of Lysias' men fall, so Lysias withdraws to Antioch to hire more soldiers. Judas and his kindred then go up to Mount Zion, find the sanctuary desolate, and appoint blameless priests to cleanse it. They pull down the profaned altar, store its stones until a prophet comes, build a new altar of whole stones, and rededicate the temple on the twenty-fifth of Chislev in the 148th year. The people establish an eight-day yearly festival of dedication, and Judas fortifies Mount Zion and Bethsura.

l: Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Judas learns of Gorgias' night march and moves to strike the king's army at Emmaus, then leads three thousand men to victory, urging them to hold off from the spoils until Gorgias' force is dealt with. He prays before meeting Lysias at Bethsura with ten thousand men, later leads the cleansing of the holy place, and fortifies Mount Zion and Bethsura.

l: Gorgias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Gorgias takes five thousand infantry and a thousand cavalry on a night march, guided by the men of the citadel, to surprise the Jews. He finds Judas' camp empty and searches the mountains, believing the Jews are fleeing, then sees the burning camp and his army flees.

l: Lysias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Lysias is told of the defeat by escapees and is confounded and discouraged that the king's commands had not been carried out. The next year he gathers sixty thousand infantry and five thousand cavalry, is defeated at Bethsura, and withdraws to Antioch to gather hired soldiers for a greater return to Judea.

l: Gorgias' army, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Gorgias' army moves out at night, finds the Jewish camp empty, and is scattered. Those in the rear fall by the sword, about three thousand are killed, and the survivors on the mountain, seeing the smoke of the burning camp, flee into the land of the Philistines.

l: Jews (Judas's followers), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Judas' army of three thousand men lacks the armor and swords they desired, yet sounds trumpets, defeats the Gentile force, and pursues it to Gazara, Idumaea, Azotus, and Jamnia. They burn and plunder the camp, taking gold, silver, blue, and sea purple, and sing thanksgiving. Later ten thousand men defeat Lysias' army at Bethsura, and the army goes up to cleanse the temple.

l: Gentiles, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: The Gentile forces are defeated at Emmaus, and Judas hopes all the Gentiles will know that one redeems Israel. They had profaned the sanctuary and altar, and the reproach of the Gentiles is turned away at the rededication. Judas fortifies Zion so they cannot trample it again.

l: Lysias' army (Lysias), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Lysias' army of sixty thousand chosen infantry and five thousand cavalry encamps at Bethsura in Idumaea. About five thousand of its men fall in battle against Judas' men, and the rest are put to flight.

l: Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Israel receives a great deliverance on the day of Emmaus and gives thanks to heaven. Judas and the congregation of Israel ordain an eight-day yearly feast of dedication of the altar starting on the twenty-fifth of Chislev.

l: God, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: God, called heaven and Savior of Israel, is invoked by Judas, who recalls the Red Sea and David's victory and asks him to remember the covenant of the fathers. The people give him thanks for the victories and for the good success at the dedication, praising him as good, whose mercy endures forever.

l: Mount Zion, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: The army goes up to Mount Zion and finds the sanctuary desolate. Judas appoints men to fight those in the citadel while the holy place is cleansed, and afterward Zion is fortified with high walls and strong towers so the Gentiles cannot trample it again.

l: sanctuary, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: The sanctuary is found laid desolate, with the gates burned, shrubs growing in the courts, and the priests' chambers pulled down. Blameless priests cleanse it, carrying the defiled stones to an unclean place, and it is rebuilt, its courts consecrated, and furnished with new holy vessels, the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table.

l: altar of burnt offerings, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: The altar of burnt offerings is found profaned by the Gentiles. The priests deliberate and decide to pull it down so it will not be a reproach, laying its stones on the temple hill until a prophet comes to give an answer concerning them.

l: new altar, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: A new altar is built of whole stones according to the law, like the former one. Sacrifice is offered on it on the twenty-fifth of Chislev, the same day the Gentiles had profaned the old one, and it is dedicated with songs, harps, lutes, and cymbals over eight days.

l: cleansing and rededication of the temple, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: After the victories, Judas and his kindred resolve to cleanse and rededicate the holy place, and the people mourn at the desolation. Blameless priests cleanse it, a new altar and vessels are made, incense is burned, lamps lit, and loaves set out, and the dedication is celebrated for eight days and made an annual observance.

l: battle at Emmaus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Gorgias' night march finds Judas' camp empty, and Judas' three thousand appear in the plain at daybreak and defeat the Gentile army, pursuing it as far as Gazara, Idumaea, Azotus, and Jamnia. About three thousand fall, the camp is burned and plundered, and Gorgias' men flee to the land of the Philistines.

l: battle at Bethsura, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: The following year Lysias encamps at Bethsura in Idumaea with a large army and Judas meets him with ten thousand men after a prayer for help. About five thousand of Lysias' men fall, and Lysias withdraws to Antioch to gather hired soldiers.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: After the Gentiles around Israel grow angry at the rededicated sanctuary and begin attacking Jews, Judas Maccabaeus campaigns against the children of Esau, the children of Baean, and the Ammonites under Timotheus. When Jews in Gilead and Galilee appeal for help, Judas and his brother Jonathan go to Gilead with eight thousand men, while Simon takes three thousand to Galilee, and Joseph son of Zacharias and Azarias are left to guard Judea with orders not to fight. Simon defeats the Gentiles near Ptolemais, and Judas takes Bosora, routs Timotheus, captures other Gilead cities, crosses the brook, destroys Carnaim, and storms Ephron, which had refused him passage, before bringing the Gilead Jews safely to Mount Zion. Meanwhile Joseph and Azarias disobey Judas's order, attack at Jamnia seeking a name for themselves, and are routed by Gorgias with about two thousand dead. Judas and his kindred are glorified, and Judas then strikes Hebron and Azotus, while certain priests who sought exploits are slain.

l: Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Judas defeats the children of Esau, the children of Baean, and the Ammonites, then leads eight thousand men with Jonathan into Gilead to rescue besieged Jews. He takes Bosora, routs Timotheus, takes Mizpeh and other cities, crosses the brook first to defeat the Gentiles, storms Ephron after its refusal of peaceful passage, and brings the Gilead Jews to Mount Zion without losing any. He is glorified among Israel and the Gentiles, then strikes Hebron and Azotus, pulling down altars and burning images before returning to Judah.

l: Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Judas tells Simon to choose men and rescue the Jews of Galilee, and he goes with three thousand men. He fights many battles, defeats the Gentiles, pursues them to the gate of Ptolemais, kills about three thousand, and brings the Galilean and Arbatta Jews to Judea with gladness.

l: Joseph the son of Zacharias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Joseph is left with Azarias as a leader of the people in Judea, with orders from Judas to fight no battle with the Gentiles until Judas returns. Hearing of the others' exploits, he wants to get a name for himself and marches toward Jamnia, where he is put to flight and pursued to the borders of Judea.

l: Azarias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Azarias is left with Joseph to lead the people and guard Judea, and is told not to fight the Gentiles until Judas returns. He joins Joseph in seeking a name, attacks at Jamnia, and is routed by Gorgias. The text says they were not of the family of those by whom deliverance was given to Israel.

l: Timotheus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Timotheus leads the Ammonite forces defeated by Judas and later commands the Gentile army besieging the strongholds in Gilead. His army flees from Judas with about eight thousand dead, and he gathers another army near Raphon, where he says Judas will defeat them if he crosses first. Judas does cross first and defeats them.

l: Gentiles, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: The Gentiles around Israel, angered by the rebuilt altar, plot to destroy the race of Jacob and kill Jews in Gilead, Galilee, and elsewhere. They are repeatedly defeated by Judas and Simon, with cities burned and many killed, and Gorgias's force defeats Joseph and Azarias at Jamnia.

l: Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Israelites in Gilead and Galilee are attacked, killed, captured, and shut up in strongholds, and they appeal to Judas for help. Those rescued are brought to Judea with their families and goods, and they go up to Mount Zion with joy and burnt offerings. About two thousand fall at Jamnia through the disobedience of Joseph and Azarias.

l: Judas's army, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Judas's army of eight thousand goes with him to Gilead, fights in three companies with trumpets and prayer, and captures several cities. It pursues Ephron's conquest, escorts the Gilead Jews home, and returns with not one man slain.

l: Judea, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Judea is guarded by Joseph and Azarias while Judas and Simon are away. It receives the rescued Jews of Galilee and Gilead, and its borders are the point to which the routed force of Joseph and Azarias is pursued.

l: Gilead, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Gilead is the land where Jews are besieged in Bosora, Bosor, Alema, Casphor, Maked, Carnaim, and other cities, and where they flee to the stronghold of Dathema. Judas conquers Bosora, Mizpeh, Casphor, Maked, Bosor, and other cities there, then removes the Jews to Judah.

l: Galilee, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Messengers from Galilee report that people of Ptolemais, Tyre, Sidon, and all Galilee of the Gentiles have gathered to destroy the Jews there. Simon goes in, defeats the Gentiles, and brings the Jews of Galilee and Arbatta to Judea.

l: Ephron, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Ephron is a large, strong city on the road home from Gilead that the army must pass through. Its people block the gates with stones and refuse Judas's peaceful offer of passage. Judas fights it a day and a night, takes it, kills all the males, razes it, and passes through over the slain.

l: Judas's campaign in Gilead, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Judas and Jonathan cross the Jordan after letters report the Gentile threat and learn from the Nabathaeans of the sieges. They capture Bosora, rout Timotheus, take Mizpeh and other cities, destroy Carnaim, take Ephron, and lead the Jews of Gilead home to Judah with no losses.

l: Defeat of Joseph and Azarias at Jamnia, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Disobeying Judas's order, Joseph and Azarias march toward Jamnia to win a name, where Gorgias comes out to meet them. They are put to flight and pursued to the borders of Judea, with about two thousand Israelites killed. The text attributes this to their not listening to Judas and his kindred.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: King Antiochus fails to plunder a rich temple city in Elymais, Persia, then hears that Judas's forces have defeated his armies, torn down the abomination at Jerusalem, and fortified the sanctuary and Bethsura. Grieving, he confesses that his evils at Jerusalem caused his misfortunes, appoints Philip to guide his son, and dies in the 149th year. Lysias sets up the young Antiochus as king, named Eupator, and when Judas besieges the citadel, ungodly Israelites appeal to the king, who marches out with a huge army and elephants. At Bethzacharias Eleazar kills the lead elephant and dies beneath it, but the king's forces take Bethsura and besiege the sanctuary, whose defenders are starving in the seventh year. Hearing that Philip has returned to seize the government, Lysias urges peace; the king swears an oath, breaks it by ordering the wall of Mount Zion pulled down, and returns to Antioch, where he defeats Philip and takes the city.

l: King Antiochus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: King Antiochus fails to pillage a rich city in Elymais, Persia, and flees to Babylon. Hearing of the defeats in Judah, he falls sick with grief, admits his evils at Jerusalem brought this on him, names Philip to oversee his kingdom and son, and dies in the 149th year.

l: Antiochus his son (Eupator), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: After his father's death, the young Antiochus is set up as king by Lysias, who raised him, and is named Eupator. He then gathers a large army, marches against Judas, accepts Lysias's counsel to make peace, breaks the oath, and returns to Antioch, where he takes the city from Philip by force.

l: Lysias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Lysias, who had earlier been put to shame by the Jews, installs Antiochus's son as king upon learning of the old king's death. When Philip returns, he persuades the king and leaders to make peace with the Jews and restore their laws, citing weakness, scant food, and affairs of the kingdom.

l: Philip (friend of Antiochus), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The dying Antiochus appoints Philip over his kingdom and gives him crown, robe, and signet ring to guide his son. Philip returns from Persia and Media with the king's forces seeking to control the government, and is found master of Antioch until the young king fights him and takes the city.

l: Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Judas plans to destroy the garrison in the citadel and gathers the people to besiege it in the 150th year, building mounds and engines of war. He then marches to Bethzacharias near the king's camp and engages the king's army.

l: Eleazar, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Eleazar, called Avaran, sees the tallest elephant in royal armor and thinks the king is on it. He charges through the phalanx, kills many, crawls under the elephant and kills it, and dies when it falls on him, giving his life for his people and an everlasting name.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Jerusalem is where the abomination on the altar was pulled down and where Antiochus recalls taking the vessels and destroying Judah's inhabitants. The king's army advances on it, encamping toward Mount Zion, and the king enters Mount Zion and orders its wall pulled down.

l: sanctuary, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The sanctuary has been surrounded with high walls as before. The king besieges it for many days with mounds and engines, but its defenders run out of food in the seventh year and most scatter, leaving few, until peace is made and they come out.

l: Bethsura, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Bethsura, fortified by the Jews, is attacked by the king's army, which is met by Jews burning its engines. Its people make peace and leave for lack of food in the Sabbath year, and the king takes it and appoints a garrison.

l: citadel (at Jerusalem), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Those in the citadel keep hemming Israel in around the sanctuary and strengthening the Gentiles. Judas besieges it in the 150th year, and some of the besieged slip out to complain to the king.

l: Jews (Judas's followers), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The Jews defeated earlier armies, took plunder, and fortified the sanctuary and Bethsura. They fight bravely, burn the king's engines at Bethsura, and counter his engines at the sanctuary, but are weakened by famine, and are then deceived by the king's oath, which is broken.

l: king's army, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The army includes 100,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, 32 elephants, and hired soldiers from other kingdoms and islands. It advances in splendor to Bethzacharias, loses 600 men in the first clash, takes Bethsura, and besieges the sanctuary until peace is made.

l: elephants (king's war elephants), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The 32 elephants are given grape and mulberry juice and distributed among the phalanxes, each with a thousand armed infantry, five hundred cavalry, and a wooden tower holding four men and an Indian driver. One, the tallest, is killed by Eleazar and falls on him.

l: siege of Jerusalem citadel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Judas besieges the citadel in the 150th year with mounds and engines of war. Some besieged men and ungodly Israelites escape and appeal to the king, prompting his campaign.

l: battle at Bethzacharias, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The king's huge army, with elephants, glittering shields, and trumpets, meets Judas at Bethzacharias, and 600 of the king's men fall. Eleazar kills an elephant and dies, and the Jews turn away from the army's strength.

l: peace treaty and its breaking, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Lysias proposes peace, allowing the Jews to follow their own laws, and the king and princes swear to it, so the defenders leave the stronghold. The king then sees the strength of Mount Zion, breaks his oath, and orders the surrounding wall pulled down.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: In the one hundred fifty-first year, Demetrius, son of Seleucus, returned from Rome, took the throne after the army killed Antiochus and Lysias, and heard accusations against Judas from Alcimus and other lawless Israelites. He sent Bacchides and Alcimus, whom he made high priest, to take vengeance; they offered deceitful peace, and Alcimus swore an oath to the Hasidaeans and then had sixty of them killed in one day. Bacchides killed more people, left Alcimus in charge and returned to the king, while Judas struck back at deserters. When Alcimus complained again, the king sent Nicanor, who tried to seize Judas by deceit, lost about five hundred men at Capharsalama, and then mocked the priests in Jerusalem and swore to burn the temple. After the priests prayed and Judas prayed at Adasa, Nicanor was the first to fall in the battle on the thirteenth of Adar, his army was destroyed, his head and right hand were hung beside Jerusalem, and the day was made an annual festival, after which the land had a few days of rest.

l: Demetrius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Demetrius, son of Seleucus, came out of Rome with a few men to a city by the sea and reigned there. He refused to see the faces of Antiochus and Lysias, so the army killed them, and he took his throne. He then sent Bacchides and Alcimus to take vengeance on Israel, and later sent Nicanor to destroy the people.

l: Alcimus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Alcimus led the lawless men of Israel who accused Judas to the king, desiring to be high priest, and Demetrius made him high priest and sent him with Bacchides. He swore peace to the Hasidaeans, after which sixty of them were killed, and Bacchides left him in charge of the country. He struggled to maintain his priesthood, and when he saw Judas had grown strong he returned to the king with evil accusations, which led to Nicanor's mission.

l: Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Judas and his kindred were accused to the king of destroying the king's friends and scattering the lawless from the land. He did not trust the deceitful peace words of Bacchides, went out through Judea to take vengeance on deserters, and avoided Nicanor once he learned of his deceit. He prayed at Adasa with three thousand men, and his army defeated Nicanor's on the thirteenth of Adar.

l: Bacchides, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Bacchides, a great man and faithful friend of the king who ruled the country beyond the river, was chosen by Demetrius to see the destruction and take vengeance on Israel. He came with a great army and sent deceitful words of peace to Judas, which were ignored. He encamped at Bezeth, seized and killed many deserters and some of the people by throwing them into a large pit, left Alcimus in charge with a force, and went back to the king.

l: Hasidaeans, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: The Hasidaeans were the first among the children of Israel to seek peace from Alcimus and Bacchides, reasoning that a priest of Aaron's seed would do them no wrong. They trusted Alcimus's oath, but sixty of them were seized and killed in one day. This broken oath spread fear among all the people.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Jerusalem was the place around which the blood of the saints was shed, and Bacchides withdrew from it to Bezeth after the killings. Nicanor came there with a great army, and the remnant of his men fled into the city of David after Capharsalama. Nicanor's head and right hand were hung up beside Jerusalem after his defeat.

l: Nicanor, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Nicanor, an honorable prince of the king who hated Israel, was sent to destroy the people and came to Jerusalem with a great army. He tried to seize Judas through a deceitful offer of peace, lost about five hundred men at Capharsalama, then mocked the priests at mount Zion and swore to burn the temple. He was the first to fall at Adasa, and his head and right hand were cut off and hung beside Jerusalem.

l: sanctuary, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: The priests showed Nicanor the burned sacrifice being offered for the king at the sanctuary, but he mocked them and swore to burn up the house if he returned safely. The priests stood before the altar and temple, wept, and prayed that God, who chose the house to be called by his name, would take vengeance on Nicanor. Nicanor fell in battle before he could carry out the threat.

l: Battle at Adasa, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Judas encamped at Adasa with three thousand men and prayed that God would crush the army as his angel had struck down one hundred eighty-five thousand blasphemers before. On the thirteenth of Adar the armies met, Nicanor was the first to fall, and his army threw away their weapons and fled. They were pursued a day's journey to Gazara and men from surrounding villages turned them back, so that all fell by the sword and none were left.

l: Day of Nicanor (festival), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: After the victory, the Jews were exceedingly glad and kept the day as a day of great gladness. They ordained that it be kept year by year on the thirteenth day of Adar. Afterward the land of Judah had rest a few days.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Judas hears reports of the Romans' power, including their conquests of the Gauls, Spain, Philip, Perseus, and Antiochus the great king of Asia, as well as their friendship toward allies and their orderly senate and yearly single ruler. Because the Greek kingdom kept Israel in bondage, Judas sends Eupolemus son of John and Jason son of Eleazar to Rome to seek friendship and alliance. The Roman senate is pleased with the request and sends back a treaty written on bronze tables to be kept in Jerusalem. The treaty pledges mutual military help between Rome and the Jews while forbidding supplies to the other side's enemies, and allows amendments by agreement. Rome also states it has written to King Demetrius, asking why he made his yoke heavy on the Jews and warning that it will do them justice and fight him by sea and land if they complain again.

l: Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Judas, also called Maccabaeus, hears of the Romans' fame, conquests, and loyalty to friends. He chooses Eupolemus and Jason and sends them to Rome to establish friendship and alliance and to free the Jews from the Greek yoke.

l: Romans, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: The Romans are described as valiant men who befriend those who join them, destroy those who oppose them, and make and depose kings, yet none wears a crown or purple. They are governed by a senate of three hundred twenty men and one yearly ruler, and they welcome the Jewish embassy, agree to the alliance, and warn Demetrius to stop oppressing the Jews.

l: Eupolemus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Eupolemus, son of John, son of Accos, is chosen by Judas as an envoy. He travels with Jason on the long journey to Rome and speaks before the senate to request an alliance.

l: Jason, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Jason, son of Eleazar, is chosen by Judas to go to Rome with Eupolemus. He helps present the Jewish request for alliance and friendship to the senate.

l: Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: The Jews, under Judas, seek Roman friendship because the Greek kingdom keeps Israel in bondage. They are registered as Rome's allies and friends, and Rome pledges to defend them against Demetrius.

l: Roman alliance treaty, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: The treaty, written on bronze tables and sent to Jerusalem as a memorial, binds Rome and the Jews to help each other in war and to give no supplies, food, weapons, money, or ships to each other's enemies. Both parties may add to or remove terms by mutual decision, and such changes are ratified.

l: Roman conquests, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Judas is told of Roman victories over the Gauls, in Spain where they took the silver and gold mines, and over Philip, Perseus, and Antiochus, who was captured with his 120 elephants and made to pay tribute and give hostages and land. Other kingdoms and islands that rose against Rome were destroyed and made servants, while those far and near feared its fame.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Demetrius sends Bacchides and Alcimus back into Judah, and at Elasa Judas, left with only eight hundred men, refuses to flee and falls in battle after routing Bacchides's right wing. His brothers Jonathan and Simon bury him at Modin, and Israel mourns. The lawless gain power under Bacchides, who persecutes Judas's friends, and the friends choose Jonathan as leader. Jonathan and Simon flee to the wilderness, avenge their brother John against the children of Jambri, escape Bacchides at the Jordan, and later hold Bethbasi against him. After Alcimus dies of a stroke and Bacchides is defeated, Jonathan makes peace with Bacchides, who returns the captives, and Jonathan begins to judge the people at Michmash.

l: Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Judas, encamped at Elasa with three thousand chosen men, was left with about eight hundred when the rest slipped away. He refused to flee, defeated Bacchides's right wing and pursued it to mount Azotus, but fell in the battle. He was buried at Modin and mourned as the savior of Israel, with his many other deeds left unwritten.

l: Bacchides, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Bacchides was sent by Demetrius with Alcimus into Judah, and he fought Judas at Elasa, where he commanded the right wing. He made ungodly men rulers, hunted Judas's friends, and pursued Jonathan to the Jordan, losing about a thousand men. He fortified cities, was later defeated at Bethbasi, swore peace with Jonathan, returned the captives, and never again entered Judah's borders.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Jonathan was chosen by Judas's friends as prince and leader after Judas died. He fled Bacchides, avenged his brother John on the children of Jambri, swam the Jordan to escape, and fortified Bethbasi. He then made peace with Bacchides, settled at Michmash, began to judge the people, and destroyed the ungodly out of Israel.

l: Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Simon helped bury Judas at Modin and fled with Jonathan to the wilderness of Tekoah. He joined the ambush of the children of Jambri. Left in charge of Bethbasi, he sallied out, burned Bacchides's siege engines, and helped defeat him.

l: Alcimus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Alcimus was sent with Bacchides into Judah and in the one hundred fifty-third year ordered the wall of the sanctuary's inner court pulled down, along with the works of the prophets. He was struck with palsy, lost the ability to speak, and died in great torment.

l: Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Israel made great lamentation for Judas and suffered greatly under Bacchides, worse than at any time since the prophets stopped appearing. After the peace with Bacchides the sword ceased from Israel, and Jonathan began to judge the people.

l: children of Jambri, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: The children of Jambri came out of Medaba and seized John and all he had. Jonathan and Simon ambushed their wedding procession, killing many and taking the spoils, which turned the wedding into mourning and avenged the blood of their brother.

l: Judas's army, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Judas's army, three thousand chosen men at Elasa, was terrified by the enemy's numbers and dwindled to no more than eight hundred. The remainder fought from morning until evening and defeated the right wing, but fled when Judas fell.

l: Bacchides's army, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Bacchides's army had twenty thousand infantry and two thousand cavalry. Its right wing was defeated by Judas, but its left wing followed and the battle turned desperate. Later about a thousand of its men fell at the Jordan, and it was defeated at Bethbasi, where its engines were burned.

l: lawless and ungodly men of Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: After Judas died the lawless emerged throughout Israel, and Bacchides made the ungodly rulers of the country. They searched out Judas's friends for vengeance, later counseled Bacchides against Jonathan, and were angrily killed in large numbers when his plan failed, with about fifty slain by Jonathan's men.

l: battle at Elasa, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: At Elasa, Judas's eight hundred men faced Bacchides's much larger army, and the fighting lasted from morning until evening. Judas routed the right wing and pursued it to mount Azotus, but the left wing followed him, many fell on both sides, and Judas was killed.

l: death of Judas, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Judas fell at the desperate battle at Elasa and the rest fled. Jonathan and Simon buried him in his ancestors' tomb at Modin, and all Israel mourned many days, saying how the mighty had fallen.

l: peace treaty (Jonathan and Bacchides), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: After his defeat at Bethbasi, Bacchides decided to leave, and Jonathan sent ambassadors proposing peace and the return of captives. Bacchides accepted, swore never to seek Jonathan's harm, restored the captives from Judah, and departed without returning to their borders.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: In the 160th year Alexander Epiphanes took Ptolemais, and King Demetrius tried to win the Jew Jonathan with a letter granting authority to raise forces, and the return of hostages. Alexander outbid him by appointing Jonathan high priest and sending a purple robe and golden crown, and Jonathan put on the holy garments at the feast of tabernacles. Demetrius then offered sweeping tax releases and privileges, but Jonathan and the people distrusted him and stayed loyal to Alexander. Alexander was defeated and Demetrius fell in battle, after which Alexander married Ptolemy's daughter Cleopatra at Ptolemais and honored Jonathan there. Later Demetrius, son of Demetrius, returned from Crete, and his officer Apollonius challenged Jonathan, who took Joppa and, with Simon, defeated Apollonius at Azotus, burned the temple of Dagon, and was rewarded by Alexander with a gold buckle and Ekron.

l: Alexander Epiphanes, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Alexander, son of Antiochus, took Ptolemais in the 160th year and reigned there. He appointed Jonathan high priest and friend, fought Demetrius, married Ptolemy's daughter Cleopatra at Ptolemais, and later honored Jonathan with a gold buckle and Ekron. He grieved and returned to Antioch when Demetrius, son of Demetrius, arrived.

l: Demetrius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: King Demetrius gathered great forces against Alexander and sent Jonathan a peace letter, then a larger offer of tax releases, control of the citadel, and funds. Jonathan and the people did not trust him because of earlier evils he had done. He fell in battle against Alexander, though the text first says Alexander's army fled.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Jonathan received Demetrius's letter, gained the hostages, and rebuilt Jerusalem's walls and Mount Zion. He accepted Alexander's appointment as high priest, wore the holy garments at the feast of tabernacles, rejected Demetrius's later offers, and was honored by Alexander at Ptolemais. He later took Joppa, won at Azotus, burned Dagon's temple, and received a gold buckle and Ekron.

l: Demetrius, son of Demetrius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: In the 165th year he came out of Crete into the land of his ancestors. His arrival caused Alexander to grieve and return to Antioch, and he appointed Apollonius over Coelesyria.

l: Apollonius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Appointed by the younger Demetrius over Coelesyria, Apollonius camped at Jamnia and sent Jonathan a taunting challenge to fight in the plain. He lost Joppa to Jonathan, then used cavalry and a hidden ambush of a thousand horsemen at Azotus, but his forces were exhausted and defeated.

l: Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Simon, Jonathan's brother, met him to help when Jonathan marched out against Apollonius. At Azotus he brought forward the army against the phalanx after the cavalry tired, and defeated them.

l: Ptolemy, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Ptolemy, king of Egypt, agreed to Alexander's request for his daughter in marriage. He came with Cleopatra to Ptolemais in the 162nd year, where Alexander wed her.

l: Ptolemais, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Alexander took possession of Ptolemais in the 160th year and was received there. Demetrius offered it as a gift to the Jerusalem sanctuary. Alexander later wed Cleopatra there and met Jonathan, whom he honored.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Jonathan returned to Jerusalem, read Demetrius's letter publicly, and rebuilt the city and walls. The citadel's men released the hostages, and Demetrius later offered to make the city holy and free. Jonathan marched from Jerusalem against Apollonius and returned there with spoils.

l: Joppa, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Joppa shut out Jonathan because Apollonius had a garrison there. After fighting, the people grew afraid and opened to him, and Jonathan became master of the city.

l: Azotus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Apollonius went to Azotus and the armies joined battle there. After his cavalry was defeated, survivors fled into Beth-dagon, and Jonathan burned Azotus, the nearby cities, and the temple of Dagon with those inside.

l: Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: The Jews were offered release from tributes, taxes, and other burdens, plus enrollment of thirty thousand in the king's forces, by Demetrius, but did not accept them, remembering his past evil. They favored Alexander, who first spoke peace to them, and remained his allies.

l: Demetrius's letter and offers to the Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Demetrius promised the Jews freedom from tributes, the salt tax, and crown levies, plus release of captives, holiness for Jerusalem, and control of the citadel. He also offered annexed districts, Ptolemais for the sanctuary, annual silver, and building costs. Jonathan and the people rejected it all out of distrust.

l: high priesthood, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Alexander appointed Jonathan high priest of his nation and king's friend, sending a purple robe and golden crown. Jonathan put on the holy garments at the feast of tabernacles in the seventh month of the 160th year.

l: battle between Alexander and Demetrius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Alexander gathered great forces and camped near Demetrius, and the two kings joined battle. Alexander's army fled and Demetrius pursued, but Demetrius fell that day as the battle continued until sunset. Alexander afterward claimed to have overthrown Demetrius and taken his throne.

l: battle at Azotus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Apollonius's cavalry surrounded Jonathan's army and shot arrows from morning until evening, while the people stood fast and the horses tired. Simon then attacked and routed them, and Jonathan burned Azotus and Dagon's temple, with about eight thousand killed by sword or fire.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: King Ptolemy of Egypt enters Syria with a large force, garrisons its cities, and turns against his son-in-law Alexander, giving his daughter to Demetrius and crowning himself king of Asia at Antioch. Alexander is defeated and beheaded by Zabdiel the Arabian, and Ptolemy dies three days later, leaving Demetrius king. Jonathan besieges the citadel at Jerusalem, wins Demetrius' favor with gifts at Ptolemais, and receives confirmation of the high priesthood and a letter of tax exemptions and added territory for Judea. When Demetrius is threatened by an uprising in Antioch, Jonathan's three thousand men save him, but he then breaks faith with Jonathan, and Tryphon brings the young Antiochus to defeat Demetrius. Antiochus confirms Jonathan's honors and makes Simon governor, and Jonathan and Simon campaign in Gaza, Bethsura and Galilee, where Jonathan rallies his routed army and defeats the foreigners at Hazor before returning to Jerusalem.

l: Ptolemy, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: King Ptolemy of Egypt gathered a great force, entered Syria with words of peace, and garrisoned the cities. He turned against Alexander, gave his daughter to Demetrius, and put on the crown of Asia at Antioch along with that of Egypt. He defeated Alexander, received his head, and died three days later.

l: Alexander, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: King Alexander was Ptolemy's son-in-law, and Ptolemy accused him of trying to kill him and coveting his kingdom. While Alexander was in Cilicia putting down a revolt, Ptolemy took his wife away from him. Alexander fought Ptolemy, was routed, fled to Arabia, and was beheaded by Zabdiel the Arabian.

l: Demetrius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Demetrius was offered Ptolemy's daughter and became king in the 167th year. He won Jonathan over with gifts, granted the Jews tax relief and territory, and then dismissed most of his troops, who came to hate him. After Jonathan's men saved him in Antioch he lied, estranged himself from Jonathan and treated him harshly, and was then routed by Tryphon and Antiochus and fled.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Jonathan met Ptolemy at Joppa, besieged the citadel at Jerusalem, and won Demetrius' favor at Ptolemais with gifts, gaining confirmation of the high priesthood and a charter of exemptions. He sent three thousand men to save Demetrius, was mistreated by him afterward, and received honors from the young Antiochus. He took Gaza's hostages, and at Hazor, after his army fled, he tore his clothes, prayed, and turned the battle to a rout of the foreigners before returning to Jerusalem.

l: Tryphon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Tryphon, formerly on Alexander's side, saw that the forces murmured against Demetrius. He persuaded Imalcue the Arabian to hand over the young Antiochus, brought him back to reign, routed Demetrius, and took the elephants and control of Antioch.

l: Antiochus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Antiochus was Alexander's young child, raised by Imalcue the Arabian until Tryphon obtained him. He was crowned king and joined the forces that routed Demetrius. He wrote to Jonathan confirming the high priesthood, appointing him over four districts, granting him golden vessels, purple and a golden buckle, and made Jonathan's brother Simon governor from the Ladder of Tyre to Egypt's borders.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Jerusalem was where Jonathan returned after escorting Ptolemy, and its citadel was under siege by him. Hostages from Gaza were sent there, and the Jews returned there with plunder from Antioch. A copy of Demetrius' grants was to be set up on its holy mountain, and Jonathan returned there after the battle at Hazor.

l: Antioch, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Ptolemy entered Antioch and put on the crown of Asia. Later its people, numbering 120,000, rose to kill Demetrius, but the Jews sent by Jonathan killed about 100,000, set the city on fire and forced peace. Tryphon afterward took control of the city.

l: Judea, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Jonathan asked Demetrius to make Judea free from tribute, promising three hundred talents. Demetrius confirmed its borders and added the governments of Aphaerema, Lydda and Ramathaim from Samaria, with the king's dues and taxes given back.

l: Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: The Jews were declared friends of Demetrius, who granted them exemptions. Three thousand Jewish men saved Demetrius in Antioch, killing about 100,000 of its people and winning glory and plunder. Demetrius later broke faith with them.

l: people of Antioch, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: The people of Antioch gathered to the number of 120,000, wanted to kill Demetrius, and seized the main streets. The Jews killed about 100,000 of them and burned the city, and they then threw away their weapons, pleaded for the king's right hand, and made peace.

l: citadel (at Jerusalem), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Jonathan gathered the Judeans and built many engines of war to besiege the citadel. Lawless men reported this to Demetrius, but Jonathan continued the siege. Later he asked Demetrius to remove the citadel's troops, since they fought against Israel continually, and Demetrius only promised to do so if he found an opportunity.

l: Demetrius' grants to the Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Demetrius' letter to Lasthenes confirmed the borders of Judea and added the three governments of Aphaerema, Lydda and Ramathaim, in place of the king's yearly dues. He also gave back the tithes, taxes, salt pits and crown taxes, declared the grants never to be annulled, and ordered a copy set up on the holy mountain. He later lied and treated Jonathan harshly.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Jonathan the high priest sends envoys to Rome and letters to the Spartans to renew friendship, citing an earlier letter from the Spartan king Arius to Onias claiming kinship through Abraham. Jonathan then confronts Demetrius' princes at Hamath, who withdraw at night, and he raids the Zabadaean Arabs and Damascus while Simon takes Ascalon's area and Joppa. Jonathan and Simon fortify Jerusalem, Judea, and Adida. Tryphon, who wants to rule Asia, lures Jonathan to Ptolemais with promises, and the people of Ptolemais seize him and kill the thousand men with him. Jonathan's remaining forces return safely to Judah, where Israel mourns and surrounding Gentiles plan to destroy them.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Jonathan the high priest sent envoys to Rome and letters to the Spartans to renew friendship, and pursued Demetrius' princes, struck the Zabadaean Arabs, and traveled through Damascus. He had Jerusalem's walls strengthened and the citadel isolated, then trusted Tryphon at Bethshan, sent most of his forces home, and went to Ptolemais with a thousand men. There he was seized, and all of Israel mourned him.

l: Rome, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Jonathan's chosen envoys entered the Roman senate house and asked to renew the friendship and alliance as in former time. The Romans gave them letters to men in every place, requiring safe conduct for them on their way to the land of Judah.

l: Spartans, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Jonathan wrote to the Spartans as kindred, recalling a letter from their king Arius to Onias stating that Spartans and Jews descend from Abraham. Arius had proposed that their livestock and goods be held in common, and Jonathan asked for a reply.

l: Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: The Jews, through Jonathan and their senate, priests and people, sought to renew brotherhood with the Spartans and friendship with Rome, saying they had been helped from heaven against their enemies. After Jonathan's capture they mourned greatly and became very afraid, and the surrounding Gentiles, saying they had no ruler or helper, sought to destroy them utterly.

l: Demetrius' princes, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Demetrius' princes returned with a larger army to fight Jonathan, and he met them at Hamath. Hearing that Jonathan's men were armed and ready, they feared, left fires burning in their camp, and withdrew across the river Eleutherus, where Jonathan failed to overtake them.

l: Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Simon traveled as far as Ascalon and its nearby strongholds, then took Joppa because he heard its people planned to hand the stronghold to Demetrius' men, and he placed a garrison there. He also built Adida in the plain, fortifying it with gates and bars.

l: Tryphon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Tryphon sought to reign over Asia and move against king Antiochus, and feared Jonathan would oppose him. At Bethshan, seeing Jonathan's large army, he instead received him honorably and persuaded him to dismiss his forces and come to Ptolemais with a few men. After Jonathan was seized there, Tryphon sent troops and cavalry into Galilee and the Great Plain to destroy Jonathan's men.

l: Ptolemais, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Tryphon promised to give Ptolemais to Jonathan, along with other strongholds, forces and officers. When Jonathan entered, its gates were shut and he was seized.

l: people of Ptolemais, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: The people of Ptolemais shut the gates when Jonathan entered, seized him, and killed with the sword all those who had come in with him.

l: Jonathan's army, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Jonathan came to Bethshan with forty thousand chosen men, then sent them home to Judah at Tryphon's request, keeping three thousand, of whom two thousand stayed in Galilee and one thousand went with him. The thousand were killed at Ptolemais, and the men in Galilee, learning of it, marched close together ready to fight, so their pursuers turned back and they reached Judah in peace.

l: alliance and friendship with Rome and Sparta, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Jonathan sent Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason to Rome to renew the former friendship and alliance, and told them to go also to the Spartans with his letters. Rome received them and gave letters for safe conduct, while the Spartan link rested on Arius's earlier letter claiming kinship.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Simon rallies the frightened people of Judah against Tryphon's invading army, fortifies Jerusalem, and sends Jonathan the son of Absalom to take Joppa. Tryphon, holding Jonathan captive, demands a hundred talents and two of Jonathan's sons; Simon pays out of fear of the people's reaction, but Tryphon does not release Jonathan, and kills him near Bascama before returning to his own land. Simon buries Jonathan at Modin and builds an elaborate monument there for his family.
