Tryphon kills the young King Antiochus and takes the crown of Asia, while Simon fortifies Judea and wins from King Demetrius a letter granting peace, tax release, and confirmation of the strongholds, which ends the Gentile yoke in the 170th year. Simon then captures Gazara, starves the Jerusalem citadel into surrender and cleanses it, and appoints his son John leader of his forces.

l: Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Simon encourages the fearful people, recalls what his family has done for the laws and sanctuary, and is accepted as leader in place of Judas and Jonathan. He pays Tryphon's ransom demand without result, buries Jonathan at Modin, builds the tomb monument, fortifies Judea, and secures peace and tax release from King Demetrius. He takes Gazara and the Jerusalem citadel, is recorded as high priest in contracts, and makes his son John leader of all his forces.

l: Tryphon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Tryphon musters a mighty army to invade Judah, holding Jonathan prisoner, and deceitfully demands money and hostages without releasing him. Turned back by heavy snow, he goes to Gilead, kills Jonathan near Bascama, and returns to his own land. He then deceives and kills the young King Antiochus, takes the crown of Asia, and brings calamity on the land; Simon later says all he did was plunder.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Jonathan, brother of Simon, is taken along under guard by Tryphon and is detained on the claim that he owes money to the king's treasury. Tryphon kills him near Bascama after being paid, and he is buried there. Simon later retrieves his bones and buries him at Modin, and all Israel mourns him many days.

l: King Demetrius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: King Demetrius answers Simon's request with a letter addressed to Simon as high priest and friend of kings. He accepts the golden crown and palm branch, confirms earlier grants and the strongholds Simon built, forgives past faults and the crown tax, releases the Jews from tribute, and offers enrollment in his court and peace.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Jerusalem is where Simon gathers the people and urges them to fight, and he hurries to finish its walls and fortify it all around. Its citadel remains in enemy hands until Simon takes it, after which the hill of the temple by the citadel is strengthened and Simon lives there.

l: Modin, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Modin is called the city of Simon's fathers, where Simon buries Jonathan's bones. There Simon builds the elaborate tomb for his father, mother, and four brothers, which the text says remains to this day.

l: Gazara, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Simon besieges Gazara with a siege engine, strikes a tower, and captures it, causing uproar. The people beg for mercy and Simon expels them, cleanses the idol houses, settles law-keeping men there, strengthens the city, and builds himself a dwelling. His son John later lives there as leader of the forces.

l: people of Judah (Simon's people), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: The people of Judah tremble at Tryphon's approach but revive when Simon speaks, and they promise to do all he tells them as their leader. Fear of their reaction leads Simon to send the ransom, and they mourn Jonathan many days. After the yoke is lifted they date contracts by the first year of Simon.

l: people of the citadel (Jerusalem citadel garrison), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: The people of the citadel ask Tryphon to come through the wilderness and send them food, but snow stops him. Cut off from the country and from trade, many die of famine, and they beg Simon for his right hand. He gives it but expels them from the citadel.

l: citadel (at Jerusalem), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: The citadel in Jerusalem is blockaded so that its occupants starve, and Simon cleanses it of its pollutions after they surrender. He enters it on the twenty-third day of the second month in the 171st year with praise, palm branches, harps, cymbals, and songs, and orders the day kept yearly with gladness.

l: tomb monument (Simon's tomb at Modin), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Simon builds the monument high with polished stone front and back, with seven pyramids for his father, mother, and four brothers. It is set with great pillars carrying suits of armor and carved ships visible to sailors, and the text says it remains to this day.

l: hostages (Jonathan's money and sons demanded by Tryphon), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Tryphon demands a hundred talents of silver and two of Jonathan's sons as hostages, claiming a debt to the king's treasury. Simon knows it is deceit but sends them so he will not be blamed for Jonathan's death. Tryphon takes the children and money but does not release Jonathan.

l: end of Gentile yoke (year 170), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: In the 170th year, following Demetrius's letter releasing the Jews from tribute, the yoke of the Gentiles is taken from Israel. The people begin writing contracts dated 'the first year of Simon, the great high priest and captain and leader of the Jews.'

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Chapter 14 opens with King Demetrius going into Media to seek help against Tryphon and being captured by Arsaces, king of Persia and Media. It then describes the peace and prosperity of Simon's rule, during which he took Joppa as a harbor, enlarged the nation's borders, took Gazara, Bethsura and the citadel, and glorified the sanctuary. Rome and Sparta, grieved at Jonathan's death, wrote on brass tablets to renew their friendship and alliance with Simon, and Simon sent Numenius to Rome with a gold shield of one thousand minas. In gratitude the people recorded Simon's deeds on bronze tablets set on Mount Zion, confirmed him as leader and high priest forever until a faithful prophet should arise, and set out his authority, including purple and gold and obedience from all. The decree, confirmed earlier by King Demetrius, was accepted by Simon, and copies were to be kept in the sanctuary precinct and the treasury.

l: Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Simon brings peace and prosperity: he takes Joppa as a harbor, enlarges the borders, captures Gazara, Bethsura and the citadel, fortifies cities, and glorifies the sanctuary. He renews the alliance with Rome and Sparta, sends Numenius to Rome with a gold shield, and is honored by the people as leader, governor and high priest, accepting the office and its prerogatives of purple, gold and universal obedience.

l: King Demetrius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: King Demetrius gathers his forces and goes into Media for help against Tryphon, but Arsaces' prince strikes his army, seizes him, and Arsaces puts him under guard. The people's decree also notes that he had confirmed Simon in the high priesthood, made him one of his friends, and honored him greatly.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: The Spartans' letter was read before the congregation at Jerusalem. Simon removed the Gentiles who had made a citadel in the city of David and polluted the area around the sanctuary, placed Jews in it, and made the walls of Jerusalem high.

l: Rome, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Rome heard that Jonathan was dead and was exceedingly grieved, then on learning Simon was high priest wrote to renew the friendship and alliance made with Judas and Jonathan. Simon sent Numenius to Rome with a great gold shield weighing one thousand minas to confirm the alliance, and Demetrius heard that Rome called the Jews friends, allies and kindred.

l: Spartans, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: The Spartans grieved at Jonathan's death and wrote on brass tablets to Simon to renew friendship and alliance. Their letter to Simon, the elders, priests and people calls the Jews kindred, and records that they received the Jewish ambassadors Numenius and Antipater honorably and put their words in the public records.

l: Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Israel rejoiced with great joy when Simon made peace in the land. The people credit Simon, his brothers and his father's house with chasing away Israel's enemies and confirming liberty to Israel.

l: Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: The Jews are called kindred by the Spartans and friends, allies and kindred by the Romans. Under Simon, Jews were placed as garrisons in Bethsura, Joppa, Gazara and the citadel at Jerusalem, and the Jews and priests were pleased that Simon be their leader and high priest forever until a faithful prophet arises.

l: people of Judah (Simon's people), The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Simon's nation tilled their land in peace, with the old men conversing in the streets and the young men in warlike apparel. They thanked Simon and his sons, proclaimed his deeds in a great congregation, made him leader and high priest, and consented to ordain that he act according to the decree.

l: sanctuary, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Simon glorified the sanctuary and added to its vessels. The decree says he and his brothers withstood enemies so the sanctuary and law might be established, and that the citadel's occupants had polluted its surroundings until Simon removed them. Simon was to take charge of it, and the tablets were to be set up within its precinct.

l: bronze tablets, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: The Spartans wrote to Simon on brass tablets to renew friendship, and the people wrote their own tablets of brass recording Simon's deeds and honors, set on pillars on Mount Zion. The people also commanded that the writing be put on tablets in a conspicuous place in the sanctuary precinct, with copies in the treasury for Simon and his sons.

l: alliance and friendship with Rome and Sparta, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Rome and Sparta renewed with Simon the friendship and alliance confirmed with Judas and Jonathan, sending letters on brass tablets that were read at Jerusalem. The Spartan letter records the ambassadors Numenius and Antipater, and Simon sent Numenius to Rome with a gold shield to confirm the alliance.

l: high priesthood, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Simon was made high priest in place of Jonathan, and the people made him leader and high priest for his faith and justice. The decree confirms the office as his forever until a faithful prophet arises, and Demetrius also confirmed it to him; Simon accepted it along with the roles of captain, governor and protector.

l: peace and prosperity under Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: The land had rest all the days of Simon: people tilled in peace, the land and trees gave fruit, and each sat under his vine and fig tree unafraid. No one was left who fought them, kings were defeated, cities were supplied and defended, and Simon's name was known to the end of the earth.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: King Antiochus, son of Demetrius, writes to Simon the high priest and the Jewish nation confirming tax remissions, the right to coin money, and the freedom of Jerusalem in return for support against Tryphon. Antiochus gathers forces, drives Tryphon to flee to Dor, and besieges the city by land and sea. Envoys led by Numenius arrive from Rome with a letter from the consul Lucius to King Ptolemy and many other rulers and countries, telling them not to harm the Jews and to hand over fugitive troublemakers to Simon. Once the siege is under way, Antiochus rejects Simon's two thousand men and annuls his earlier covenants, then sends Athenobius to demand Joppa, Gazara and the Jerusalem citadel or one thousand talents. Simon refuses and offers one hundred talents, Tryphon escapes by ship to Orthosia, and Antiochus appoints Cendebaeus to attack Judea, where he fortifies Kidron and raids the highways.

l: Antiochus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Antiochus, son of Demetrius, writes to Simon promising tax remissions, coinage rights and great honor, and gathers forces that leave Tryphon with few men. He besieges Dor, then rejects Simon's help, cancels their covenants, and demands the cities or money through Athenobius. Angered by Simon's reply, he appoints Cendebaeus against Judea and pursues Tryphon.

l: Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Simon, the high priest and governor, receives Antiochus's letter and the Roman letter written to him, and sends two thousand chosen men with silver, gold and arms to Antiochus, who refuses them. He impresses Athenobius with his wealth and attendance, and answers the demands by saying the lands are the fathers' inheritance, offering one hundred talents for Joppa and Gazara.

l: Tryphon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Tryphon is left with few men when Antiochus's forces gather against him, and he flees to Dor, knowing his forces have deserted him. Shut up in Dor by the siege, he later escapes by ship to Orthosia while Antiochus pursues him.

l: Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: The Jewish nation is addressed in Antiochus's letter, which confirms their tax remissions and right to coin money. Their ambassadors had renewed friendship with Rome and brought a gold shield, and Rome's letter tells the kings not to harm them. Under Cendebaeus, the people of Judea are later raided, taken captive and killed.

l: Dor, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Dor, a city by the sea, is where Tryphon flees as his forces desert him. Antiochus encamps against it with 120,000 men and 8,000 cavalry, and ships join the attack so that no one can go in or out.

l: Athenobius, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Athenobius, a friend of Antiochus, is sent to Simon to demand Joppa, Gazara and the Jerusalem citadel or payment. He is amazed at Simon's glory in Jerusalem, gets no answer to give after Simon's counter-offer, and returns in a rage to report to the king.

l: Joppa, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Joppa is named by Antiochus as a city of his kingdom held by Simon, and he demands its return. Simon replies that it and Gazara did great harm to the people and offers one hundred talents for them.

l: Gazara, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Gazara is named by Antiochus as one of the cities of his kingdom that Simon holds, and he demands it back. Simon says it harmed the people of the country and offers one hundred talents for it together with Joppa.

l: Judea, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Judea is the land where Antiochus claims Simon has done harm, and Simon says it is the fathers' inheritance. Antiochus orders Cendebaeus to encamp against it, and Cendebaeus comes from Jamnia to invade it, capture and kill people, and raid its highways from Kidron.

l: Cendebaeus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Cendebaeus is appointed chief captain of the sea coast by Antiochus, with infantry and cavalry. He is ordered to fight the people of Judea, and he comes to Jamnia, provokes and invades, takes captives, kills people, and builds up Kidron with cavalry and infantry for raiding.

l: siege of Dor, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Antiochus besieges Dor with 120,000 men and 8,000 cavalry, bringing up engines of war and ships from the sea to cut off all movement in or out. Tryphon is shut up there before escaping by ship to Orthosia.

l: demand for cities or payment, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Through Athenobius, Antiochus demands that Simon hand over Joppa, Gazara and the Jerusalem citadel, plus tributes, or pay five hundred talents for the cities and five hundred more for the harm done, or face attack. Simon refuses, saying the land is the fathers' inheritance, and offers one hundred talents for Joppa and Gazara, which enrages the king.

l: Roman letter of protection for the Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Brought by Numenius from Rome, the letter from the consul Lucius to King Ptolemy says the Jews' ambassadors renewed the friendship and gave a gold shield of one thousand minas. It tells the kings not to fight the Jews or ally with their enemies, and to hand fugitive troublemakers to Simon, and the same message goes to many other rulers and countries.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 16
s: John reports from Gazara that Cendebaeus is acting against Judea, and the aged Simon sends his two oldest sons, Judas and John, to fight for the nation. John leads twenty thousand men to defeat Cendebaeus's army near a brook by Modin, pursues it to Kidron and the towers of Azotus, burns them, and returns in peace. Ptolemy son of Abubus, governor of the plain of Jericho and the high priest's son-in-law, plots to seize the country. He receives Simon and his sons Mattathias and Judas at the stronghold of Dok in the eleventh month of the 177th year, and kills them at a banquet. Ptolemy then writes to the king for forces and sends men to kill John at Gazara and to seize Jerusalem, but John learns of it, kills the men sent against him, and the chapter closes by pointing to the chronicles of his high priesthood.

l: John, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 16
s: John went up from Gazara to report Cendebaeus's actions to his father Simon, then led the army with his brother Judas, pursuing the defeated enemy to Kidron and burning the towers at Azotus before returning to Judea in peace. After Ptolemy murdered his father, John was warned at Gazara, seized the men sent to kill him and killed them. His other deeds, wars and wall-building are said to be written in the chronicles of his high priesthood, which he held after his father.

l: Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 16
s: Simon, now old, sent his two oldest sons Judas and John to fight in his and his brother's place, recalling the battles of Israel his family had fought since youth. While visiting the cities of the country, he went down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas in the 177th year, eleventh month (Sebat). Ptolemy received him deceitfully at Dok, and Simon was killed at a banquet.

l: Cendebaeus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 16
s: Cendebaeus's actions prompted John's report to Simon, and he met the Jewish army with a great force of infantry and cavalry across a brook. His army was put to flight, with many wounded to death and the rest fleeing to the stronghold. He had built Kidron, to which John pursued his forces.

l: Ptolemy, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 16
s: Ptolemy son of Abubus was governor of the plain of Jericho, rich in silver and gold, and son-in-law of the high priest. His heart was lifted up and he planned to master the country, so he deceitfully received Simon and his sons at Dok, and killed Simon and two sons at a banquet. He then wrote to the king for forces, sent men to kill John at Gazara, summoned the captains of thousands with promises of gifts, and sent others to take Jerusalem and the temple hill; the text calls his deed a great iniquity repaying evil for good.

l: battle against Cendebaeus, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 16
s: Twenty thousand men of war and cavalry went out under John, slept at Modin, and met Cendebaeus's large force across a brook in the plain. John crossed first, encouraging the fearful men to follow, and placed the cavalry among the infantry. At the sound of the trumpets Cendebaeus's army fled, Judas was wounded, John pursued to Kidron and burned the towers at Azotus, and about two thousand enemy fell.

l: banquet and murder of Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 16
s: Ptolemy received Simon and his sons Mattathias and Judas into the small stronghold of Dok, which he had built, and gave a great banquet with men hidden there. When they had drunk freely, Ptolemy and his men took their weapons, rushed in, and killed Simon, his two sons and some servants. The text condemns it as a great iniquity, evil repaid for good.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: The Jews of Jerusalem and Judea write a letter to the Jews of Egypt, praying for their welfare and urging them to keep the feast of tabernacles in the month Chislev in the 188th year. They recall their earlier letter from the time of distress after Jason and his company revolted, and thank God for rescuing them, including the death of Antiochus, who was cut down by the priests of Nanaea's temple in Persia. They explain that the feast marks the purification of the temple and remembers the altar fire in Nehemiah's time. The godly priests had hidden the fire in a dry well before the exile to Persia, and Nehemiah's men found only a thick liquid there, which, sprinkled on the sacrifice, kindled a great blaze when the sun shone. The Persian king enclosed and sanctified the place, and the liquid was called Nephthar, meaning Cleansing.

l: Jews in Jerusalem and Judea, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: They send greetings and a letter to the Jews in Egypt, together with the senate and Judas, addressed also to Aristobulus. They pray for the Egyptian Jews, recall their own suffering and prayers being heard, thank God for deliverance, and urge them to keep the feast of tabernacles in Chislev in the 188th year.

l: Jews in Egypt, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: They are the recipients of the letter from Jerusalem and Judea, which includes Aristobulus, King Ptolemy's teacher, of the stock of the anointed priests. They are prayed for and told to keep the feast of tabernacles in the month Chislev and to remember the fire given in Nehemiah's time.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: He is asked to do good to the Egyptian Jews, remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and give them willing hearts. He heard the prayers of the Jews in their distress, saved them from great perils, and threw their enemies out into Persia. In Nehemiah's prayer he is addressed as Creator, King, and savior of Israel, and is asked to accept the sacrifice, gather the scattered, and punish oppressors.

l: Antiochus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: He came into the temple of Nanaea in Persia with an army and a few friends, on the pretense of marrying her so as to take a large part of the treasures as a dowry. The priests locked him in and killed him, cutting him and his company to pieces and throwing their heads to the people outside.

l: priests of Nanaea's temple, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: They set out the treasures and, when Antiochus entered with a small company, locked the temple. They opened a secret door in the paneled ceiling, threw stones, struck down the prince, and cut him and his company to pieces by treachery.

l: Nehemiah, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: Having received a charge from the king of Persia, he sent descendants of the priests to seek the hidden fire, and when they found thick liquid he had it drawn out and sprinkled on the wood and sacrifices. A great blaze was kindled, he led or joined in the prayer, and he had the rest of the liquid poured on large stones. He and his companions called the liquid Nephthar, meaning Cleansing.

l: fire (from the altar), The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: It was taken by the godly priests and hidden in a waterless well before the exile to Persia. Later it was found to be thick liquid, which when sprinkled on the sacrifice and exposed to the sun produced a great blaze that consumed the offering. The letter urges the Egyptian Jews to remember it.

l: godly priests of that time, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: When the fathers were about to be led into Persia, they took some of the altar fire and hid it secretly in the hollow of a dry well. They made sure that no one knew the place.

l: thick liquid (Nephthar), The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: It was found in the well where the fire had been hidden, and Nehemiah had it sprinkled on the wood and sacrifices, which then burst into a great blaze when the sun shone. Poured on large stones, it flamed but went out when the light from the altar shone back. The Persian king enclosed the place, gave some of the liquid as presents to those he favored, and it was named Nephthar, meaning Cleansing, though most call it Nephthai.

l: feast of tabernacles, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: The Egyptian Jews are told to keep it in the month Chislev in the 188th year. It is linked to the coming celebration of the temple's purification on the twenty-fifth day and to remembering the fire given in Nehemiah's time.

l: purification of the temple, The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees / Chapter 1
s: The Jews in Jerusalem are about to celebrate it in Chislev on the twenty-fifth day. They notify the Egyptian Jews so that they may keep a feast of tabernacles at the same time.
